Brief facts of the case are as under:
The plaintiff has filed the present suit for partition and separate possession of her alleged 1/8th share in the suit schedule properties and for consequential declaration that the Sale Deed dated 30.05.2005 and the Gift Deed dated 31.03.2011 are not binding on her share.
It is the case of the plaintiff that she and defendant Nos.1 to 7 are the children of late C. Venkatamuni and constitute a Hindu Undivided Joint Family governed by Mitakshara law.

According to her, the suit schedule properties are ancestral and joint family properties derived from ancestral nucleus and income, including compensation received from acquisition of ancestral lands.

The plaintiff further contends that during the lifetime of late Venkatamuni, certain properties were alienated and some properties were purchased in the names of defendant Nos.2 and 8 out of joint family funds.
It is alleged that the Sale Deed dated 30.05.2005 and the Gift Deed dated 31.03.2011 were executed without her knowledge and consent and are not binding on her share.
She asserts that despite repeated demands, the defendants have failed to effect partition, thereby compelling her to file the present suit.

13. On the other hand, the contesting defendants deny the existence of joint family nucleus and contend that the suit properties are self-acquired properties of late Venkatamuni and also of defendant Nos.2, 6 and 8.
They further contend that certain properties were purchased and developed by them by raising loans and from their independent income.

It is also contended that the alienations and transfers effected are valid and binding, and that the plaintiff is not entitled to any Geetha V vs Prema V on 26 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124066794/

sentences.text:
Upon a careful consideration of the pleadings and the oral and documentary evidence adduced,
and upon due appreciation of the same, this Court proceeds to answer the issues as under:
Issue No.1: The plaintiff has pleaded that she and defendant Nos.1 to 7 are the children of late C.Venkatamuni and that they constitute a Hindu Undivided Joint Family governed by Mitakshara law.
In support of the said contention, the plaintiff has produced Ex.P.2, the genealogical tree, and Ex.P.3, the death certificate of late Venkatamuni.
The said documents clearly disclose the relationship between the parties and the fact that late Venkatamuni is the common propositus.
The oral evidence of PW-1 also reiterates that the plaintiff and defendant Nos.1 to 7 are the children of late Venkatamuni and were living as members of a joint family.
Though PW-1 was subjected to cross-examination, nothing material has been elicited to discredit her testimony on the aspect of relationship and status of the family.
15. The DW-1 during his cross-
examination
has categorically admitted that his parents are Venkatamuni and Lakshmamma and that there were eight children in the family.
He has further admitted that during the lifetime of his father, the latter was managing the affairs of the family.
These admissions clearly establish not only the relationship between the parties but also the existence of a family unit under the management of the propositus.

16. On appreciation of pleadings and the documentary evidence, it is clear that the relationship between the parties as children of late Venkatamuni is not in dispute and there is also no evidence on record to show that there was any prior partition in the family or that the joint family status had been disrupted before the filing of the suit.

Hence, on a careful consideration of the pleadings,
documentary evidence in the form of Ex.P.2 and Ex.P.3, and the clear admissions elicited in the cross-examination of DW-1, this Court is of the considered opinion that the plaintiff has successfully proved that she is a member of the joint family headed by the propositus late C. Venkatamuni as on the date of the suit.
Accordingly, this Court answers the Issue No.1 in the Affirmative.

17. Issue Nos.2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and Addl. Issue No.1: Since all these issues revolve around the suit schedule properties, the source of their acquisition, and the validity of the documents set up by the defendants, they are taken up together for common consideration.

The case of the plaintiff is that all the suit schedule properties are joint family properties derived from ancestral nucleus, including agricultural lands belonging to the grandfather Chinnamuniyappa and compensation received upon acquisition of such lands.

It is her contention that the properties,
though standing in the names of late Venkatamuni and certain defendants, were in fact acquired out of joint family funds.

Per contra, the contesting defendants contend that the properties are self-acquired properties of late Venkatamuni and also of defendant Nos.2, 6 and 8, and that Schedule 'B' properties in particular were purchased and developed out of their independent income and by raising loans.

sentences.text: At the outset, the existence of joint family nucleus is required to be examined.

The plaintiff has relied upon Ex.P.16, the award, and Ex.P.17, the certificate issued by the Special Tahsildar, which establish that late Venkatamuni received compensation of Rs.49,722/- in the year 1985 upon acquisition of ancestral lands.
The oral evidence of PW-1 further discloses that the family possessed agricultural lands and derived income therefrom.
19. The admissions of DW-1 in cross-examination are significant.

He has admitted that his grandfather possessed properties in Tamil Nadu, that compensation was received upon acquisition,
and that such financial assistance supported the family.
It is also categorically admitted that all the suit schedule 'A' to 'D' schedule properties are ancestral properties and not self acquired properties of his father.
He has further admitted that the income of his father alone was not sufficient to maintain the large family.
These admissions clearly establish the existence of ancestral nucleus and availability of joint family fund.
That when the existence of joint family nucleus is established, the burden shifts upon the person asserting self-acquisition to prove that the property was acquired without the aid of such nucleus.
20. In respect of Item No.1 & 2 of the Schedule "A" properties the plaintiff has produced documentary evidence.
The Ex.P.24 evidences that Item No.2 of Schedule 'A' property was purchased in the year 1985 in the name of Venkatamuni.
The timing of the purchase immediately after receipt of compensation under Ex.P.17 strongly probabilises that the property was acquired out of joint family funds.
No evidence is placed by the defendants to show independent income sufficient for such acquisition.
Similarly, Item No.1 stands in the name of Venkatamuni, and in the absence of proof of exclusive income, the presumption of joint family property prevails.
Thus, Item Nos.1 and 2 of Schedule 'A' are held to be joint family properties.

21. Further, insofar as Item No.4 of Schedule 'A' property is concerned, though the plaintiff has contended that the said property originally formed part of the joint family estate, the material on record clearly establishes that the same was alienated by late Venkatamuni under a registered Sale Deed dated 30.05.2005 marked at Ex.P.5.

The present suit has been instituted only in the year 2013,
after a lapse of about eight years from the date of alienation.
The plaintiff has neither pleaded nor proved the specific date of knowledge of the said transaction so as to save limitation.
22. It is pertinent to note that the sale deed in question is a registered document.

As per Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 readwith Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908,
registration of a document operates as constructive notice to the world at large.

Therefore, the plaintiff is deemed to have notice of the said alienation from the date of its registration itself,
irrespective of her actual knowledge.
In such circumstances, the right to challenge the alienation accrued on the date of execution and registration of the sale deed i.e., 30.05.2005.
Under Article 58 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a suit for declaration has to be filed within three years from the date when the right to sue first accrues.
The plaintiff having failed to institute the suit within the prescribed period, the claim in respect of Item No.4 is clearly barred by limitation.
Hence, even assuming that the said property was originally joint family property, the plaintiff has lost her right to question the alienation.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Prem Singh v. Birbal (2006) 5 SCC 353 has held that a registered document carries presumption of validity and limitation runs from the date of Geetha V vs Prema V on 26 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124066794/
10 execution unless fraud is specifically pleaded and proved.
In the instant case the plaintiff has neither pleaded fraud nor explained delay.
Though Item No.4 was alienated prior to the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, the plaintiff's claim fails not on that ground but on limitation.
Hence, this Court holds that the Item No.4 of Schedule 'A' property is not available for partition.
23. In respect of Schedule 'B' Properties (Item Nos.1 and 2) the defendants have contended that these properties are self-acquired properties of defendant Nos.2 and 8.
However, the evidence on record does not support this contention.
The Ex.P.5 discloses that a joint family property was sold on 30.05.2005.
Ex . P.6 and Ex.P.14 disclose that properties were purchased shortly thereafter in 2005 and 2006.
The proximity of these transactions raises a strong inference that the sale proceeds were utilized for subsequent purchases.
24. The DW-2, who claims ownership over Item No.2 of Schedule 'B', has admitted that she is a housewife and has no documentary proof of independent income or financial assistance from her parents.
She has also admitted that she does not know the details of the transactions.
These admissions weaken her claim of self- acquisition.
Similarly, DW-1 has failed to establish that defendant No.2 or 8 had sufficient independent income at the relevant time.
Further, though Ex.D.2 and Ex.D.4 disclose that loans were availed for development of the properties, they do not establish that the properties were originally purchased from independent funds.
They only show that subsequent improvements were made.
25. It is settled position of law that the burden of proving self-acquisition lies heavily on the person who asserts it and must be established by clear and cogent evidence.
In the present case, such burden has not been discharged.
Therefore, Schedule 'B' properties, including Item No.2 claimed by defendant No.8, are held to be joint family properties.
26. In respect of the Schedule 'C" property the defendants have set up a plea that the property belonging to Lakshmamma was bequeathed under a Will.
However, the defendants have neither produced the alleged Will nor examined the attesting witness to prove the Will.
The DW-1 during his cross examination has admitted that the property stood in the name of his mother and that she had not alienated the same during her lifetime.
The RTC extracts also show that the property continued in her name.
Therefore, in the absence of proof of the Will as required under law, the same cannot be accepted.
The defendants failed to prove the Will as per Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act and Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act.
That, Schedule C Property being the self-acquired property of Lakshmamma, upon her intestate death, it devolves under Section 15 of the Hindu Succession Act.
Therefore, Schedule 'C' property devolves upon all legal heirs and is available for partition.

27. In respect of the schedule "D" property the Defendant No.6 has contended that Schedule 'D'
property is his self- acquired property.
However, he has failed to produce any documentary evidence to show sufficient independent income at the time of acquisition.
On the contrary, in his cross-examination, he has admitted that he had limited income and has not produced documents to substantiate his earnings.

The proximity of purchase with other transactions and the existence of Geetha V vs Prema V on 26 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124066794/
11 joint family nucleus support the plaintiff's case.
Therefore, Schedule 'D' property is also held to be joint family property.
28. The Gift Deed at Ex.P.25 is relied upon by the defendants.
As per Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, a document required by law to be attested must be proved by examining at least one attesting witness.
However, the execution of the said document has not been proved in accordance with law and no attesting witness has been examined.
Further, the surrounding circumstances create suspicion..
Hence, the Gift Deed cannot be held to be validly proved and is therefore not binding on the plaintiff.
29. It has come on record through Ex.D.2, Ex.D.4 and the oral evidence that defendant Nos.2, 6 and 8 have raised loans and developed certain properties by constructing buildings.
However, such development does not alter the character of the properties as joint family properties.
It is settled law that improvements made by one co-parcener do not confer exclusive ownership but may entitle such person to equitable adjustment at the time of partition.

30. On a careful and detailed appreciation of the oral admissions of DW-1 and DW-2, the documentary evidence produced by both parties, and the settled principles of law laid down in landmark judgments, this Court holds that the plaintiff has successfully proved the existence of joint family nucleus and that the suit schedule properties, except the item No.4 of schedule "A" property,
are joint family properties.

The defendants have failed to prove that Schedule 'B' properties,
including Item No.2 claimed by defendant No.8, are their self-acquired properties.
The alleged Will and Gift Deed are not proved in accordance with law and are not binding on the plaintiff.
The development of properties by defendant Nos.2, 6 and 8 does not defeat the plaintiff's right but is subject to equitable adjustment.

Therefore, in view of the above findings and observations this Court answers the Issue No.2 is answered in partly Affirmative, Addl.Issue No.1 in Affirmative and Issues Nos. 3, 4, 5 and 6 are all answered in the Negative.
31. Issue Nos.7 and 8:
These issues are interconnected and arise out of the findings recorded on Issue Nos.2, 4, 5 and 6 regarding the nature of the properties and validity of the documents relied upon by the defendants.
Hence, they are taken up together for common consideration.

The plaintiff has sought declaration that the Sale Deed dated 30.05.2005 and the Gift Deed dated 31.03.2011 are not binding on her share, and has further sought partition and separate possession of her 1/8th share in the suit schedule properties.

In view of the findings recorded on the earlier issues,
this Court has held that the suit schedule properties, except Item No.4 of Schedule 'A' property, are joint family properties.

It is also held that the defendants have failed to prove that Schedule 'B' and 'D' properties are their self-acquired properties and that the alleged Gift Deed has not been proved in accordance with law.
Insofar as the Sale Deed dated 30.05.2005 relating to Item No.4 of Schedule 'A' property is concerned, this Court has already held that the challenge to the said alienation is barred by limitation.
Consequently, the plaintiff is not entitled to any declaration or share in respect of the said property.

No attesting witness has been examined and the circumstances surrounding the execution create suspicion.
Therefore, the said Gift Deed cannot be held to be binding on the plaintiff's share.

Further, once the properties are held to be joint family properties,
the plaintiff, being a daughter of late Venkatamuni, is entitled to claim equal share as a coparcener.
The law in this regard has been settled by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma reported in (2020) 9 SCC 1,

Accordingly, this Court holds that the plaintiff is entitled to 1/8th share in Item Nos.1 and 2 of Schedule 'A' properties, Schedule 'B', Schedule 'C'
and Schedule 'D' properties.
33. Further, at the same time, it has come on record that defendant Nos.2, 6 and 8 have developed certain portions of the properties by raising loans and putting up construction.
However, such development does not change the character of the properties nor extinguish the plaintiff's right.
The law is well settled that improvements made by one co-sharer do not confer exclusive ownership but only entitle such person to equitable adjustment at the time of partition.
Therefore, the equities arising out of such development shall be considered at the stage of final decree proceedings.

Thus,
the plaintiff is entitled for declaration to the limited extent that the Gift Deed dated 31.03.2011 is not binding on her share, and is further entitled for partition and separate possession of her 1/8th share in the suit schedule properties, except Item No.4 of Schedule 'A' property.
Accordingly, this Court answers Issue Nos.7 and 8 partly in the Affirmative.
34. Issue No.9:

In view of the above discussion and findings on the above issues, this Court proceeds to pass the following:-
ORDER
The suit of the plaintiff is partly decreed with costs as per the terms below:

The plaintiff is declared entitled to 1/8th share in Item Nos.1 and 2 of Schedule 'A'
properties, and Schedule 'B, C & D' properties.
The claim in respect of Item No.4 of Schedule 'A' property is dismissed as barred by limitation.
The relief sought by the plaintiff in respect of the Sale Deed dated 30.05.2005 is rejected, as the challenge to the said alienation is barred by limitation.
The Gift Deed dated 31.03.2011 are declared not binding on the plaintiff to the extent of her share.
The equities arising out of improvements and developments made by defendant Nos.2, 6 and 8 shall be worked out in the final decree proceedings.
Draw preliminary decree accordingly.
